title: The SGPC, 1920
hook: Sikhs formed a committee to manage gurdwaras and a volunteer band, the Akali Dal

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhagat Singh, and your line was an honest mind. Did you thank someone for saying it straight? Today, back to the gurdwaras, and the outrage over the robe turns into a plan. Day nine hundred eighty-three.

Four letters, printed on signboards and letterheads in Punjab: S, G, P, C. You can pass them without a second look. Behind them is a long name, the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, and behind the long name is a question Sikhs had been asking since the robe was given to the general. Who should look after the gurdwaras? In 1920, at a gathering in Amritsar, Sikhs gave their answer. We will. Today: the SGPC.
screen: `FOUR LETTERS ON SIGNBOARDS.` → `A LONG NAME BEHIND THEM.` → `WHO LOOKS AFTER THE GURDWARAS?`

segments.voice: First, the problem. Gurdwaras were then often in the hands of mahants, hereditary custodians, and some treated the shrines and their lands as private property. Some practices crept in that reformers said went against the Gurus' teaching, and at the Golden Temple the manager answered to the government. Second, the committee. In 1920 Sikhs met in Amritsar and formed a committee to take over the management of the gurdwaras on behalf of the Panth, the whole Sikh community. Its long name means, roughly, the chief committee for managing the gurdwaras. Third, the volunteers. Alongside it came a band of volunteers called the Akali Dal. Akali comes from Akal, the Timeless One, a name for God, and the volunteers were called Akalis. They were not paid soldiers. They were farmers, teachers, former servicemen and students who gave their time, and later their bodies, to the work. Fourth, why it's seva. Guru Nanak says, at Ang 26 of the Guru Granth Sahib, that if you serve in this world, you'll be given a seat in the court of the Lord. The reform movement was political, and the SGPC later became a powerful elected body. But at the start it ran on seva: ordinary people offering to do the job no one was paying them for. That's today's line.
screen: `SHRINES TREATED AS PRIVATE PROPERTY.` · `A COMMITTEE FOR THE WHOLE PANTH.` · `AKALIS: VOLUNTEERS OF THE TIMELESS.` · `SERVE IN THIS WORLD.` · then, large: `VOLUNTEERS STEPPED UP.`

segments.voice: Two minutes to choose one task. Sit, and let your breath settle. Think of the places you belong to: a home, a workplace, a street, a gurdwara, a club. In one of them, there's a job nobody wants. The dishes after the meal. The chairs after the meeting. The form no one fills in. Picture it clearly. Now picture yourself quietly doing it, with no one asking. Breathe slowly, and decide on one task you'll take on. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
The SGPC. The Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, formed by Sikhs to manage their gurdwaras, with a volunteer band, the Akali Dal, beside it. Today's word.
Your line: volunteers stepped up. Today, do the one task you chose, the one nobody asked you to do. Day nine hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: The SGPC today manages historic gurdwaras in Punjab and neighboring regions, including the Golden Temple; Sikhs also do seva in gurdwaras everywhere as volunteers, in the kitchen, cleaning and looking after shoes.

notes: Year 1920 is from the index title; the exact meeting (Akal Takht, November 1920) and the Akali Dal's formation date are left general. Please confirm.
'Gurdwaras were then often in the hands of mahants' uses 'many' about shrines, not people; confirm or soften.
The gloss of Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee as 'roughly, the chief committee for managing the gurdwaras' and of Akali from Akal: confirm.
The list of volunteers' backgrounds (farmers, teachers, former servicemen, students) is general; confirm.
The description of the mahants should be checked for fairness: the script says 'some', not all.
The SGPC's present scope in howItsDone (Punjab and neighboring regions): confirm wording.
